1\.**Expected Truth Lag E(L) by Wait Time: History vs. Live**   
![][image1]  
The three E(L) decay curves closely align: regardless of whether ground-truth labels are derived from post-hoc archives (dump) or real-time streams (stream), and across both the historical baseline (history) and live windows (live / live\_ext), the vast majority of label flips occur within the first 15 minutes to 1 hour and largely converge after 24 hours. This demonstrates the strong robustness of our streaming latency model across different data sources and time windows.

2\.**Expected Truth Lag E(L) by Edit Burst Intensity**   
![][image2]  
Contrary to the intuition that high-traffic edit bursts prolong instability, high-burst revisions (10+ concurrent edits) exhibit the fastest E(L) decay—dropping below 0.5 within just 5 minutes and reaching \\approx 0.25 by 1 hour. During trending events or active edit wars, high visibility attracts immediate scrutiny from active editors and automated patrolling bots, leading to rapid reversion of damaging edits. Conversely, low-burst revisions (0 or 1 concurrent edits) experience a significantly longer truth lag, as lower-traffic articles receive less immediate oversight and often require several hours to a full day (6 h–1 d) before erroneous edits are detected and corrected.  

3\.**Revert Rate%  Across Different Editor Types**   
![][image3]  
Editing quality exhibits a sharp disparity across different editor types. Temporary/anonymous users experience a high revert rate of 25.6%, as they lack permanent accounts or long-term community commitment, often leading to more casual or lower-quality contributions. In contrast, registered users drop significantly to 3.5%, while automated bots achieve near-zero error at 0.8% due to routine cleanup tasks executed by well-tested scripts. This empirical evidence proves that platform friction is driven primarily by low-quality temporary edits rather than overall workload.

4\.**Reconciliation Disparity: Stream vs. Dump**   
![][image4]  
Reconciliation analysis shows that both methods have their own blind spots. Offline dumps capture more historical revisions (325 cases) because they scan the whole archive. On the other hand, real-time streams catch 66 revisions that dumps completely miss—these are fast, short-lived reverts happening between snapshot gaps. This proves that neither method alone is enough; we need both streaming and dumps to see the full picture.

**5.Rows Below K-Anonymity Threshold**  
![][image5]

The k-anonymity analysis shows a clear difference between hourly groups and page-level summaries. At k=5, only 3.95% of hourly rows fall below the threshold, compared with 98.4% of page-summary rows. As the threshold increases to k=20, the percentages rise to 33.4% and 100%, respectively. This shows that hourly aggregation provides stronger privacy protection, while page-level release has much higher disclosure risk.

  **6\. Revert-Rate Bias (Percentage points) by Suppression Rule**  
![][image6]

The suppression analysis shows that stricter suppression rules can introduce greater bias into the released revert rates. Rules A and B produce between 6.43 and 9.19 percentage points of bias across cohorts, while Rule C produces between 14.21 and 17.26 percentage points. This demonstrates the trade-off between stronger privacy protection and the accuracy of the released data.
